categories.name: Output Risks
categories.tagline: Damages the artifact. Catch it, fix it.

categories.name: Process Distortion
categories.tagline: Damages the project. The work still ships mediocre.

categories.name: Overtrust
categories.tagline: Damages your judgment. Erodes slowly, quietly.

categories.name: Accountability
categories.tagline: Damages the field. Not reversible by you alone.

traps.title: Aesthetic Homogenisation
traps.description: When everyone uses the same models and similar prompts, the output converges. AI-generated charts start sharing the same gradients, the same rounded corners, the same safe colour palettes. Individual style disappears. The work looks competent and interchangeable, which is another way of saying it looks like nothing.
traps.todo: Develop and maintain a personal visual language that isn’t AI-derived. Use AI for speed, but make your final aesthetic choices by hand. If your chart could have come from anyone’s prompt, it’s not finished.

references.label: Zhou & Lee (2024) — Generative AI, Human Creativity, and Art, PNAS Nexus

traps.title: Context Collapse
traps.short: Assumes a similar, generic audience every time.
traps.description: AI doesn’t know your audience, your client, your publication’s norms, or the political sensitivity of the data. It makes generic charts for a generic viewer. A chart about maternal mortality in rural India and a chart about smartphone sales get the same visual treatment unless you intervene.
traps.todo: Always ask who is going to look at this, and what’s at stake for them. Provide that context in your prompt, then evaluate the output through that lens yourself. AI can’t hold the audience in mind. You can.

references.label: Marwick & boyd (2011) — I Tweet Honestly, I Tweet Passionately: Context Collapse

traps.title: Data Hallucination
traps.description: AI can invent data points, fabricate statistics, and generate plausible-sounding numbers that have no basis in your dataset. That’s confabulation, not a calculation error. A chart can end up showing a trend that doesn’t exist.
traps.todo: Never trust a number AI gives you without checking it against the source. If AI produced both the analysis and the chart, verify the analysis independently. A beautiful chart built on fake data is worse than no chart at all.

references.label: Ji et al. (2023) — Survey of Hallucination in Natural Language Generation, ACM Computing Surveys

traps.title: Anchoring
traps.short: First draft is the chosen direction.
traps.description: AI’s first output sets the frame for everything that follows. If AI generates a blue bar chart, your revisions will probably be variations on that blue bar chart: different shade, different layout, same basic idea. The first suggestion narrows your design space before you’ve explored it.
traps.todo: Generate several alternatives in your first prompt: ask for five very different approaches. Or better, sketch your own ideas before seeing AI’s. Once you’ve been anchored, it’s hard to un-anchor.

references.label: Tversky & Kahneman (1974) — Judgment under Uncertainty: Heuristics and Biases
Rastogi et al. (2022) — Deciding Fast and Slow: The Role of Cognitive Biases in AI-Assisted Decision-Making

traps.title: Satisficing
traps.description: Accepting the first “good enough” output and stopping. AI makes it easy to reach 70% quality in seconds, and that 70% looks convincingly done. The last 30% (the refinement, the specificity, the weird detail that makes a chart memorable) is what you skip because the quick version already looks like a deliverable.
traps.todo: Set a rule: AI’s first output is a draft, never a deliverable. Always do at least one round of refinement where you push beyond what AI gave you. The gap between generated and designed is where your value lives.

references.label: Herbert Simon (1956) — Rational Choice and the Structure of the Environment

traps.title: Prompt Fixation
traps.short: Focus shifts from designing to improving prompts.
traps.description: Spending more and more time refining prompts instead of doing actual design work. You tweak wording, add constraints, restructure your instructions. The activity feels productive because you’re getting different outputs each time, but prompt engineering is negotiating with a machine, not designing.
traps.todo: Set a time limit on prompting. If three rounds of prompts haven’t given you what you need, stop prompting and start making. Open Figma. Open a notebook. The fastest path to a good chart is often your own hands.

references.label: Desmond & Brachman (2024) — Exploring Prompt Engineering Practices in the Enterprise

traps.title: Speed–Quality Confusion
traps.short: Fast and good aren't the same thing.
traps.description: AI makes things fast. Speed feels like progress. But fast output and good output are different things, and AI collapses the distinction. You can produce twenty chart variations in ten minutes and feel more productive than spending two hours on one considered design, even when the single design is better work.
traps.todo: Judge your output by quality, not quantity or speed. Ask: is this chart clearer, more honest, or more useful than what I would have made without AI? If the answer is no, the speed didn’t help.

references.label: Dell’Acqua et al. (2023) — Navigating the Jagged Technological Frontier (BCG + Harvard)

traps.title: Competence Illusion
traps.short: Highest confidence is in areas you know the least.
traps.description: AI output looks polished and confident even when it’s wrong. A chart with clean axes, good typography, and a smooth colour palette can still show the wrong numbers. The surface quality hides the errors underneath, and because it looks like something a competent person made, you trust it more than you should.
traps.todo: Check the data behind any AI-generated chart before you judge the design. Read axis labels, verify totals, spot-check individual data points against the source. If you can’t verify it, you can’t publish it.

references.label: Vasconcelos et al. (2023) — Explanations Can Reduce Overreliance on AI Systems During Decision-Making
Rozenblit & Keil (2002) — The Misunderstood Limits of Folk Science: An Illusion of Explanatory Depth

traps.title: Automation Bias
traps.short: Trusting machine to be always right.
traps.description: The tendency to trust the output of an automated system over your own judgment, even when your judgment is right. If AI says “use a stacked bar chart” and your instinct says slope chart, you’ll probably go with AI anyway: it’s a system, and systems feel objective, whether or not the reasoning holds up.
traps.todo: Treat AI suggestions the way you’d treat a junior colleague’s suggestion: worth hearing, worth interrogating, never worth accepting without thinking. Your instinct earned its place.

references.label: Parasuraman & Manzey (2010) — Complacency and Bias in Human Use of Automation

traps.title: The “Looks Right” Trap
traps.short: Familiar isn't the same as accurate.
traps.description: AI generates a chart that visually resembles something you’ve seen in the New York Times or the Economist. You feel reassured. But visual resemblance to a credible source doesn’t mean the content, encoding, or data behind it is accurate. Familiar form creates false trust.
traps.todo: Ask yourself: why does this look right? Is it because the data encoding is correct, or because the styling reminds me of something trustworthy? These are two different questions. Answer both.

references.label: Vasconcelos et al. (2023) — Explanations Can Reduce Overreliance on AI Systems During Decision-Making

traps.title: Sycophantic Confirmation
traps.short: It just tells you what you want.
traps.description: AI tends to agree with you. If you ask “is this a good chart?”, it will almost always say yes and list reasons why. That’s flattery dressed up as feedback.
traps.todo: Prompt for criticism specifically: “What’s wrong with this chart? Give me three problems.” Or better yet, show your work to a real human who will disagree with you. AI is a bad critic because it wants to please you.

references.label: Sharma et al. (2023) — Towards Understanding Sycophancy in Language Models
Perez et al. (2022) — Discovering Language Model Behaviors with Model-Written Evaluations

traps.title: Cognitive Offloading
traps.short: Letting it think so you don't have to.
traps.description: When a tool can think for you, you stop thinking for yourself. If AI suggests chart types, you stop considering alternatives. If AI writes the annotation, you stop forming your own interpretation. The parts of your brain that do that work get quieter. You haven’t lost the ability. You’ve stopped practising it.
traps.todo: Form your own opinion before you ask AI for one. Sketch three chart ideas by hand before prompting. Write your headline before generating one. Use AI to expand your thinking, not replace it.

references.label: Risko & Gilbert (2016) — Cognitive Offloading, Trends in Cognitive Sciences

traps.title: Skill Atrophy
traps.short: Muscles you stopped using fade away.
traps.description: Cognitive offloading, but over months and years. If you always let AI handle colour selection, data wrangling, or code, your own ability to do those things deteriorates. The real risk: when AI gets it wrong, you no longer have the skill to notice.
traps.todo: Keep a short list of skills you refuse to delegate fully. Do them by hand regularly, even when AI could do them faster. Treat it like physical exercise: the point is capacity, not efficiency.

references.label: Bainbridge (1983) — Ironies of Automation
Budzyń et al. (2025) — Endoscopist Deskilling Risk After Exposure to Artificial Intelligence in Colonoscopy, The Lancet Gastroenterology & Hepatology

traps.title: Creative Learned Helplessness
traps.short: Forgetting you can start from nothing.
traps.description: After relying on AI for ideation repeatedly, you start to believe you can’t generate ideas on your own. “I’m not the creative one, AI is.” This is a self-reinforcing loop: the less you try, the more you feel you need AI, the less you try. Particularly dangerous for students still building creative confidence.
traps.todo: Start every project with your own ideas, even bad ones, even half-formed ones, before opening any AI tool. Protect the habit of generating from scratch. You can always use AI later. But the ability to start from nothing is yours to lose.

references.label: Seligman & Maier (1967) — Failure to Escape Traumatic Shock
Cui & Khan (2026) — AI Dependency and Academic Motivation in Higher Education: The Mediating Role of Learned Helplessness and the Moderating Role of AI Literacy, Frontiers in Psychology

traps.title: The Black Box Excuse
traps.description: “I don’t know why AI did that” becomes a way to avoid responsibility for your own design decisions. If a chart misleads, you point to the tool. But your name is on the work. You chose to use the output. You chose not to verify. “AI made it” is an admission that you gave up editorial control, not a defence.
traps.todo: If you can’t explain every choice in your chart, from the encoding to the scale to the annotation, it’s not ready to publish. Own every pixel, even the ones AI placed there. Especially those.

references.label: Elish (2019) — Moral Crumple Zones: Cautionary Tales in Human-Robot Interaction

traps.title: Attribution Erosion
traps.short: Losing track of whose idea it was.
traps.description: After iterating between your ideas and AI’s suggestions, you lose track of what came from you and what came from the model. This is a practical problem, not just an ethical one: if you can’t tell what’s yours, you can’t build on your own strengths or develop a recognisable body of work.
traps.todo: Keep a log. Even a rough one. Note which ideas started with you and which came from AI. Over time, this helps you see your own patterns and protect what makes your work yours.

references.label: He et al. (2025) — Which Contributions Deserve Credit? Perceptions of Attribution in Human-AI Co-Creation, CHI 2025
